Artificial intelligence is about to sweep through the economy. The Federal Reserve is bracing for impact.
"We are at a hinge point in the U.S. economy," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said at a conference he convened in San Francisco on Monday. But exactly when and how the economy could turn, and what that means for interest rates and inflation, isn't yet clear.
The meeting of Warsh's AI task force saw the new Fed chairman publicly asking the questions Americans will ultimately expect him to answer. He hinted at a few of his private views on whether white-collar workers could soon face massive job losses, but he largely left the speculation to an array of experts he has assembled to advise the Fed.
With the technology racing ahead, Warsh won't be able to put off giving his own answers much longer. AI lab Anthropic plans to price the shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday and could raise as much as $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Vast spending from AI firms is prompting the Fed to contemplate raising interest rates in December to slow down the rate of price increases as the tech sector heats up the economy.
Meanwhile Americans are souring on some aspects of the technology. The Nov. 3 midterms saw voters enact an array of state-level measures to slow down construction of the data centers that are essential to powering AI.
Warsh moderated three out of four sessions at Monday's event and was involved in selecting the speakers. Among them was one of the few prominent Democrats who was willing to speak out against that anti-data center trend.
It is "a very troubling sign" that so many anti-data center measures passed in the midterms, Gina Raimondo said. She is a former secretary of commerce under President Joe Biden and a former governor of Rhode Island.
Stopping AI "would be very bad for America" and for the people who voted for the measures, Raimondo said.
Warsh didn't say whether he shares that view, and how it would translate into monetary policy isn't exactly clear.
The event was an unusual one for the Fed. The central bank employs a small army of Ph.D. economists who can rapidly weigh in on anything affecting the U.S. and global economies. But in keeping with his longstanding critiques of the Fed as insular and outdated, Warsh has chosen to draw expertise from outside the institution to help it figure out how to think about what AI will do to productivity and jobs.
Warsh has assembled a task force on that issue, alongside four others devoted to aspects of Fed policymaking.
The public heard Monday from one of the three official members of the task force: venture capitalist Marc Andreessen. Warsh went to Stanford University with Andreessen's wife, and the two have been longtime friends. Another task force member, Stanford economist Chad Jones, is on leave and working at Anthropic and couldn't speak during the company's blackout period ahead of the IPO. The third, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, didn't attend the event.

New Zealand’s central bank warned on Tuesday that global financial stability risks continue to rise, with growing vulnerabilities in the non-bank lending sector driven by increased private credit activity.
In its semi-annual Financial Stability Report, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) said non-bank lenders are becoming more active in the country, particularly in commercial property and development financing.
While greater competition offers benefits for borrowers, it creates risks that are harder for the RBNZ to monitor, as much of this activity falls outside the regulated sector, it said.
Read more: Private Credit and Stablecoins Pose Risks Beyond Size, BoE Governor Bailey Warns
“While systemic risks from non-bank lenders in New Zealand remain limited given their size, their growing role in credit provision highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring,” the report said.
Banks continue to account for the majority of lending to households and businesses in New Zealand, with direct finance and non-bank lending firms representing only about 6% of overall lending, official data showed. Private credit funds and non-bank lenders are not directly regulated by the RBNZ, which also serves as the country’s banking regulator.
The RBNZ highlighted how the recent failure of an Australian property developer exposed several private lenders to potential losses, with some funds restricting withdrawals amid increased redemption requests.
Last week, Australia’s corporate regulator said it would launch an official probe into the A$3.4 billion ($2.30 billion) collapse of Sydney homebuilder Bathla, putting fresh scrutiny on the fast-growing private credit sector, which has increasingly stepped in to finance developers as banks retreat from riskier lending.
The financial stability report also warned that heightened geopolitical tensions and financial market fragility had increased global risks, with Middle East tensions disrupting energy and trade flows.
However, the report said New Zealand’s financial system remained resilient.
“Domestic financial stress has generally eased from its peak last year but remains uneven,” RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said.
Despite some narrowing of lending margins, New Zealand’s banks are maintaining strong capital and liquidity positions, with recent stress tests showing banks and insurers could withstand severe financial shocks, Breman added.
($1 = 1.4813 Australian dollars)

The defunding of weather observation systems across the world as countries focus on military spending is making it harder to predict extreme events at a time when the planet is reaching unprecedented heat levels.
Weather and climate observations worth about $10 billion globally are at risk, according to the World Meteorological Organization. Key measurements have already declined and others could be interrupted, said the WMO’s Secretary-General Celeste Saulo, in an interview on the sidelines of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. (Editor’s note: This article was published by Bloomberg on Nov. 11).
“Geopolitical tensions have resulted in a large majority of governments redirecting their investments to defense, instead of observing and understanding the climate system and preparing to adapt to it,” Saulo said. In terms of observations, she added, “We are increasingly far from solving a problem that’s not hard to solve.”
Data gathered in hundreds of weather stations across the world are essential to allow forecasters to make predictions on storms, heat waves and drought. They also feed into early-warning systems that can alert populations just before disasters strike. In addition, scientific models depend on that information to make long-term projections of how man-made global warming will impact the planet.
Because climate investment from developed countries is falling, “everything points to a decline in adaptation funding in 2026 and 2027 that will have a great impact on observation systems,” Saulo said. “Many countries in the Global South have no resources to invest.”
The risk that the US will defund global ocean observations is of particular concern, she said, because no other country has the capacity to deploy resources to gather ocean data at a similar scale. A halt in these observations would lead to a so-called single point of failure, in which the ocean observations system collapses.
“Everyone assumes the system will keep functioning as it has for the past 20 years, but that’s not the case,” she said. “When the system stops working, it will be too late.”
The WMO Global Climate Observing System, which assesses the state of global climate observations, needs $500 million a year to operate, while coordination efforts with different agencies cost about $10 million a year. Developing nations need a combined $150 million a year to strengthen their observation systems, the WMO estimates. All of that is under threat, Saulo said.
“These are not unimaginable sums,” she added. However, “private sectors and philanthropists are not assuming that responsibility either.”
Lack of funding is an issue across the whole UN climate system. The UN Framework Convention for Climate Change has warned it needs more money to facilitate increasingly large events like COP31 and to provide the growing amount of reports countries are asking for.
“We face challenges — mandates are growing, funds are shrinking,” the UN climate body’s Executive Secretary Simon Stiell said in his opening speech at COP31. “Serious work is needed with parties on our budget consultations over the next six months. We cannot keep doing more with less.”

Japan will create a network across the Asia-Pacific region to promote development of early-warning systems aimed at bolstering protections against extreme weather events and natural disasters.
Gaps in capabilities such as remote sensing and cellphone alerts have been highlighted by recent events, including the devastating August floods near the Nepal-China border, which killed more than 1,400 people and wiped out towns, border posts and hydropower plants
“The network will share knowledge and expertise in the introduction and operation of the early warning systems and promote effective deployment,” Japan’s Environment Minister Hiroyoshi Sasagawa said Tuesday in a speech to the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkey.
Japan, which lies on an arc of volcanoes and fault lines surrounding the Pacific Basin known as the “Ring of Fire,” has been a pioneer in earthquake early-warning systems and developing buildings designed to withstand powerful tremors.
The country also remains committed to supporting countries with climate finance, though sees a need for other nations to contribute more, Sasagawa said.
“To meet the needs of countries requiring support, it is essential to broaden the contributor base to include countries capable of contributing, and to expand various financial flows including private finance,” he said at the conference.
Developed economies have persistently called for the likes of China, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states to expand their climate finance contributions, while those nations argue that most responsibility should rest with countries that industrialized first.

Brittanye Rimpson, whose children formerly attended Raytown public schools, wants to address the school board about bullying in the district and the public comment policy at board meetings (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon)
Katty Henry said she’d like to speak to the Raytown school board about her concerns with the district, things like bullying and school safety, “if they’d let me.”
But after hearing about other residents’ struggles to be heard at recent board meetings, she has felt like it wouldn’t even be worth it to try to sign up for public comment.
Henry is raising her grandchildren, who attend Raytown schools.
Last month, she attended a small protest outside the district’s administrative building as a school board meeting took place inside. The protesters were objecting not only to bullying in district schools, but also to the fact that they haven’t been allowed to publicly address the board about it.
“I know they’re probably not going to let too many people speak,” Henry said, “but they should let some people speak.”
When school boards offer members of the public the opportunity to speak at their meetings, they generally impose limits on time, subject matter and the number of speakers who can participate in a given meeting. Many districts, including Raytown, require that public comments be related to items already on the board meeting agenda.
So if residents want to comment on bullying in schools, that would first need to be included as an item on the school board’s agenda.
But for several years now, state law has required school boards to offer residents a pathway to add items to their agendas. The process isn’t necessarily fast, but the law doesn’t list many reasons boards can refuse the requests after the resident jumps through a few procedural hoops — primarily meeting with the superintendent “to attempt a resolution of the issue.”
In Raytown, though, the board has recently denied two residents’ requests without directly citing any of the reasons specified in law — and in its own policy on adding agenda items. Another resident had a request that was denied in 2024 after she pressed the board for a response and accused it of ignoring her request entirely, according to public records that The Beacon requested and reviewed.
The records cover the period from when the district most recently updated its policy in 2023, after the law change, to the present. They show no successful requests to add agenda items.

Burton told The Beacon that the board always wants to hear from residents, but that sometimes concerns are best handled through another process, such as various committees. [Editor’s Note: This Community Voices article was written by Daan Oxener, who is a Dutch entrepreneur and tennis player who somewhat accidentally found his way into Kapchorwa’s running culture. Since 2016, he has explored Mount Elgon’s many trails and everyday community life. Through Home of Friends Guesthouse and Run Kapchorwa, he helps adventurous travelers discover the people and stories behind Uganda’s Land of Champions.]
The moment you climb the tarmac road to Kapchorwa, Uganda, you are surrounded by rolling green hills, banana plantations, and small farms. There is little sign that you are approaching one of East Africa’s elite running hubs. Kapchorwa’s first impression is rural and rustic. No tartan running tracks or fancy facilities here.
Alvin, an ambitious U.K. runner with Ugandan roots, describes his first experience of running on Kapchorwa’s trails:
‘‘The trails are very scenic. You cross small villages and rivers. The trail surfaces are made of mud with small rocks, but they are quite smooth. You see a lot of farm life. You come across the locals, children walking to school. Nothing extravagant.’’
But in this unassuming environment, international athletes are pushing their limits. And so did Alvin.
‘‘Because of my excitement to find elite athletes, I pushed myself more than I should have. I was struggling to keep pace with a group of local runners. Later I was told that Jacob Kiplimo, the world half marathon and cross-country champion, was in this group.’’
Running in Kapchorwa is challenging and takes time to adapt to. We see this with almost every international runner who comes here for the first time. The rule, therefore, is simple: Change the altitude, but leave everything else the same.
Compared with the famous running hub of Iten, Kenya, its counterpart across the border, Kapchorwa is greener and hillier. The two places share ancestral Kalenjin roots, reflected in similarities in culture and food. In terms of infrastructure, however, they are quite different: Iten has more tarmac roads, and its running tourism infrastructure is more developed, with gyms and swimming pools catering to visiting athletes.
The Mount Elgon Rainforest
‘‘Give us the forest back, and we give Uganda more champions.’’
This recurring message from elders in the Mosopisiek community says a lot about the roots of Kapchorwa’s running culture.
In 1992, when the Ugandan portion of Mount Elgon National Park was officially gazetted, many Mosopisiek people were relocated from the rainforest to the lower flanks of the mountain.
This meant a big change in their way of life: from running for miles after stolen cows to settling in one area and growing potatoes or onions; from eating forest berries and mushrooms to eating grains and plantains.
But those roots have not disappeared. You can still experience them on trail runs and hikes through the stunning, undulating landscape.
Daily endurance, or “building stamina” as the natives often describe it, starts from a young age. Children walk kilometers to school. In their free time, they jump over steep rocks and mountain streams.
The terrain itself is a training ground.

Today’s big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash
Apple (AAPL) stock trades at 36.0 times its earnings over the last twelve months, counted as normalized net income plus stock-based pay after tax, with the shares near their highest close of the past year. That is a high price for one year of profit, so it is worth setting against the profit expected over the next two fiscal years. So what sales and profit does that price assume Apple will deliver?
Apple Investors Bet On Higher Sales At Thinner Margins
The consensus forecast projects Apple’s revenue will reach $528 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with the $479 billion reported for fiscal 2026. Forecasted net income rises far less, moving to $135 billion from $132 billion. Those figures leave a net margin of 25.6% in fiscal 2027, below the 27.6% Apple reported for fiscal 2026.
For fiscal 2028, the forecast models a 7.4% increase in revenue and a 10.3% rise in net income. That puts the net margin at 26.3%, still short of fiscal 2026. The bet is on more sales, not on more profit from each dollar of sales.
On that forecast, you pay 38.0 times the average analyst estimate of Apple’s net income for fiscal 2027. That is not measured the same way as the 36.0 times trailing figure, which adds stock-based pay after tax to normalized net income. On fiscal 2028 earnings the price is 34.4 times, though that year’s forecast is uncertain: the gap between the highest and lowest per-share estimates is 23.8% of the average.
How Fast Has Apple Actually Been Growing?
Apple’s latest year ran faster than the forecast: revenue increased 15.1% in fiscal 2026, after 6.4% growth in fiscal 2025. The consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 works out to about 10% growth. Neither forecasted margin surpasses what the company has already reached: Apple reported a net margin of 26.9% in fiscal 2025 and posted a higher margin in fiscal 2026.
The iPhone led that growth, with sales rising 21.2% in fiscal 2026. Services, Apple’s second-largest business, grew 13.0%.
Management guidance points to a slower start for fiscal 2027. Apple expects December quarter revenue to grow 7% to 10%. Management said this range reflects constrained supply, noting that revenue grew 16% in the same quarter a year before. The company also expects a gross margin of 45% to 46%. Management said most of the margin decline from the September quarter comes from higher memory costs.
Where Could Apple Fall Short Of The Forecast?
Supply is the first place. Management expects memory to constrain the Mac and iPad in the December quarter because demand has been higher than it expected. Apple provides no outlook beyond that quarter. If those constraints last, the fiscal 2027 sales forecast could come down.
The cost of memory is the other place. Beyond the December quarter, management sees memory prices still rising and expects less help over time from memory already in inventory. Price increases on the Mac, iPad and iPhone have offset some of that impact, but further cost rises could push Apple’s net margin below the forecast.
If the forecast holds, the forward multiples are a fair picture of Apple’s price. Supply is where the forecast is most likely to fall short, and lower sales alongside rising memory costs would leave the stock priced for profit Apple may never earn, a riskier bet. Voters mark their ballots on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Alaska, Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
The U.S. Senate took a first step Tuesday toward reviving the moribund Federal Election Commission, holding a confirmation hearing on President Donald Trump’s nominees to lead the campaign finance watchdog after it was sidelined for the midterm elections.
The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on complaints or issuing advisory opinions. As its backlog of work has grown, candidates and political groups have been left uncertain about when — or if — the FEC will take action on alleged violations of federal campaign finance law.
The Senate Rules and Administration Committee on Tuesday weighed the nominations of two Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson, to join the FEC. Only two commissioners, both Democrats, are currently serving and the agency needs a bipartisan quorum of at least four to take official action.
“Restoring the commission’s ability to function is especially important following the 2026 midterm elections,” said Sen. Bill Hagerty, a Tennessee Republican who chaired the hearing.
Hagerty pointed to the backlog of complaints and the need to prepare for the 2028 presidential race. Restoring a quorum will allow the FEC “to resume its essential responsibilities,” he said.
The FEC enforces federal campaign finance laws and assists candidates and donors in complying with them. The FEC, which marked its 50th anniversary in 2025, also makes public a vast trove of campaign finance data.
The hearing marked an effort by Republicans to end the FEC’s dormancy during the Senate’s lame-duck period before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. At that point, Democrats will have much more power to demand that the White House nominate individuals acceptable to Democrats or block Trump’s nominees.
Democrats support restoring a quorum on the FEC, but they question whether Trump will allow commissioners to act independently.
In February 2025, Trump fired the Democratic chair of the FEC, Ellen Weintraub, who had been a commissioner since 2002. Weintraub has said she doesn’t view the firing as legally valid, though she hasn’t challenged the dismissal in court.

“Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life. I scrolled past the phrase recently on social media: Somebody had designed it with colors and typography and posted it, apparently finding resonance in the sentiment.
I chuckled a little upon seeing it. If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”
This new reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept. I’ve been running on and off for more than 50 years, some 85 percent of my life. I jogged along with my older brother when I was a girl, competed in high school as a teen, trained for a sub-3 marathon as a working professional in my 30s, plodded with a baby jogger in my 40s. Now, past 60, running has shape-shifted again. The transformation is different this time, the lessons deeper and, frankly, a little harder to grasp. But after a period of struggle, I’ve made peace with it. Because as usual, if you dare to listen, running will speak to you.
Most of us who run spend years or even decades seeking to improve, from a 5K to 10K, from breaking 4 hours in a marathon to then trying for 3:45. For a long time, wherever you are, improvement is possible, and change generally trends in one direction. Not every run, of course. The body has good days and challenging ones; that variability is a given, and progress is not a straight line. But we can expect a trajectory that provides a satisfactory feedback loop, one of betterment.
Inevitably, aging will bend the line of progression into an arc. We can know that and still have trouble seeing it at first, because the heavy legs or knee catching feels like just another hard day. Nothing a little rest or cross-training can’t solve.
If seeing it is difficult, accepting it can be even harder. The forward march has been the natural state of things for so long. The battle waged for incremental increases in mileage or decreases in time was never easy. Shouldn’t I be pushing past this? Isn’t it what runners do?
Running taught me to be tough. For years, that served me even beyond the sport. In work, the tug of fatigue from long nights at the ad agency felt familiar and manageable as a long run. Giving birth called back the discipline of breathing through pain; the years of motherhood to come called in the lessons of patience, of quietly putting in the hours without immediate affirmation or result. I loved being a badass in the endurance sport of life. The ability to override tiredness felt powerful. I enjoyed telling myself I was fine when evidence pointed to the contrary. I relished pushing against edges and limits.

During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.
“Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”

“I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she said. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”
Finding her stride
As a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.
In her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.
"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.
The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.
As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.
In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.
"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.
Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.
She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. "I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

JPMorgan Chase (JPM) said Tuesday that longtime CFO Jeremy Barnum will step down next year in the latest change among the top ranks of the country's largest bank as it prepares for CEO Jamie Dimon's eventual succession.

The announcement of Lake's departure also came as JPMorgan said it was elevating executives Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh to the role of co-president, signaling their leads to eventually take the reins from Dimon, who was expected to stay for three more years as CEO, according to an executive familiar with the matter who spoke to Yahoo Finance at the time.

De Best, 43, joined JPMorgan in 2006 and has held senior positions across investment banking, markets and corporate banking. She will also join the firm's operating committee when she assumes the CFO role.

Charlie Bilello Calls Leveraged Single-Stock ETFs ‘One of the Worst Financial Innovations’
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Charlie Bilello went after one of Wall Street’s fastest-growing product lines on November 16, 2026. In a post on X, Bilello wrote: “One of the worst financial innovations: Leveraged and inverse single-stock ETFs. -38% median investor return. >$500 million in management fees collected.”
Bilello was quoting Peter Mallouk, who pointed out that investors can now choose from 600+ ETFs linked to a single stock. Many of them add leverage, and their median expense ratio is 1% a year. Mallouk’s point was that ETFs won investors over by offering diversification and low fees. These funds put all the risk on one stock and charge more for it.
How Daily Resets Quietly Eat Returns
A leveraged single-stock ETF tries to deliver a multiple, usually 2x, of one stock’s move for a single day. An inverse fund tries to deliver the opposite of that move. The word that matters is daily. These funds reset their exposure every session, so over weeks or months their returns drift away from a simple multiple of what the stock did.
Here’s a simple example. Say a stock rises 10% one day and falls 10% the next. The stock ends down 1%. A 2x fund gains 20% and then loses 20%, which leaves it down 4%. This drag is called volatility decay. It gets worse as the stock gets choppier, and the funds tend to track the most volatile names in the market.
Fees make it worse. The GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF (NASDAQ:NVDL) has a net expense ratio of 1.64%[1], according to its prospectus. Then there is investor behavior. Traders tend to pile in after a big run and bail out after a sharp drop, locking in losses at the worst moments. That pattern helps explain why Charlie Bilello puts the median investor return at -38%. Over the same period, Charlie Bilello says the funds collected more than $500 million in management fees.
Why Leveraged Funds Clash With Retirement Goals
Income investors need two things: capital that compounds and cash that keeps coming. Leveraged single-stock funds work against both. They pay little or no real income, they experience decay, and a deep drop takes years of normal returns to recover. These funds are built as day-trading tools, a poor match for most retirement goals.

What Did Reddit Tell Investors On Its Q3 Call?
Search referral traffic, the visitors search engines send to Reddit, fell meaningfully in the third quarter, management said on the call. The decline sped up late in the quarter, management said. The shares lost 29.2% on October 30, the day after the call. That marked their largest one-day fall of the past year.
Management said on the call that the drop in search traffic appears to come from Google’s rollout of AI Mode. It said people still want Reddit, and Google is just not sending them there the way it used to. Management also said 80% of Reddit’s monetization happens in its app and among logged-in users. So the search warning on the call was about how many people reach Reddit, not about the ads it has already sold. On the same call, management guided fourth-quarter revenue growth below the third quarter’s pace.
Did Reddit’s Earlier Falls Of This Size Pay Off?
Since March 2024, Reddit stock has fallen more than 40% over 30 trading days three times. The latest, on November 2, 2026, came partway through this slide. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Clark Howard was blunt on his November 16 show. If your savings sit at JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction), Bank of America (NYSE:BAC), Citigroup (NYSE:C) or Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC), the syndicated consumer money host told listeners, “you hate your money. You absolutely hate your money.”
He also gave the reason. “The biggest banks are going to pay you 1/100th of 1% on your savings,” he said, while “the US Treasury will pay you 5.51% on your savings.”
On $10,000, that works out to about $1 a year versus roughly $551. That gap is what you give up by leaving cash where it sits.
Howard Is Right About the Banks, and Treasury’s Numbers Back Him
My conclusion: Howard’s attack on big-bank savings rates holds up. His I bond pitch also works, but only for money you can lock away for at least a year. If you put your emergency cash into I bonds, you can’t get it back when an emergency hits.
TreasuryDirect confirms a 5.51%[1] rate on I bonds issued from November 1, 2026 to April 30, 2027. That rate combines a 1.4% fixed rate with a 2% semiannual inflation rate.
The fixed rate matters most, because Treasury says it never changes[1]. Bonds bought from July through October locked in just 0.9% fixed. Buy today and you lock in 1.4% above inflation for up to 30 years[1].
On $10,000, that extra half point adds about $50 a year on top of inflation.
The alternatives pay less. The FDIC’s national average 12-month CD yields 1.8%[2], and the 52-week Treasury bill recently yielded 4.55%. The I bond pays about 3 times the average CD.
Here is an example one-year comparison on $10,000. It assumes the I bond rate holds for the full year and ignores compounding:
Even after giving up roughly $138 in lost interest, the I bond still pays more than the average CD. The interest also escapes state and local income tax[1], and you can put off federal tax until you cash the bond in.
When You Need the Cash Decides Whether This Helps or Hurts
Treasury lets you cash in an I bond only after 12 months[1]. If you cash it in before five years, you lose the last 3 months of interest[1]. Howard said the same thing on air: “You have to own them for a minimum of a year.”
Say your transmission fails in month seven. Your I bond money is frozen, so the repair goes on a credit card that charges far more than the bond earns. Cash you might need belongs in an online savings account. Howard said those accounts can pay “as much as 400 times” what the megabanks pay.
Money you won’t touch for five years is a different story. There is no penalty, and you earn inflation plus 1.4%.
Remember that the 2% inflation piece looks back and resets every six months.
In the year through September, consumer prices rose about 3.7%, roughly double the Fed’s 2% goal. If inflation cools, the rate falls.
If the inflation piece drops to zero, you earn only the 1.4% fixed rate, which is less than today’s average CD. Howard has said he would consider cashing in I bonds in a very low inflation cycle.
His 30-year warning comes with a catch. “From that point forward, I earn nothing. Nothing. Not a penny,” he said. TreasuryDirect pays electronic bonds automatically[1] when they mature, so that risk mostly applies to old paper bonds.

Iron Mountain NYSE: IRM is counting on cross-selling digital services, asset lifecycle management and data center capacity to its established customer base as it expands beyond records storage, Chief Financial Officer Barry Hytinen said at a J.P. Morgan services event.
Hytinen said the company serves more than 240,000 business customers, including 95% of the Fortune 1000. J.P. Morgan’s Alex Hess said fewer than 5% of Iron Mountain’s customers currently buy more than one service, with most using its traditional records management offering.
Growth businesses target existing customers
Iron Mountain’s digital solutions business now generates more than $600 million in revenue, compared with less than $200 million a few years ago, Hytinen said. More than 40% of its revenue is recurring, up from approximately 10% to 12% when he joined the company nearly seven years ago.
The company’s asset lifecycle management business, which handles end-of-life and refresh processes for IT equipment, generated approximately $40 million in revenue in 2021. Hytinen said it is expected to generate about $1 billion this year, reflecting both organic growth and acquisitions.
He said the business could eventually generate billions of dollars in annual revenue and become Iron Mountain’s largest revenue segment in the foreseeable future. The company also decommissions equipment for cloud hyperscalers, wiping data from devices and reselling parts.
Those customers overlap with Iron Mountain’s data center leasing clients. Hytinen said the data center business is expected to generate more than $1 billion in revenue this year, with signed leases providing a path to more than $1.7 billion on an annualized basis over time.
Data center development focuses on pre-leasing
Hytinen said Iron Mountain generally develops data centers in major cloud and inference markets rather than large AI training campuses. Its markets include Northern Virginia, Phoenix, London, Frankfurt, Mumbai, Chennai and Singapore.
The company operates approximately 540 megawatts of capacity, about 98% of which is leased, he said. Nearly 650 megawatts of additional capacity is expected to be energized over the next few years and is not yet leased. About half is expected to be energized in the next 18 to 24 months, and roughly two-thirds of the nearly 650 megawatts is in Virginia.
Hytinen described Iron Mountain as primarily a pre-lease builder. The company typically seeks to sign leases 12 to 14 months before power becomes available and begins major construction roughly nine to 10 months before energization. It may do site preparation before signing a lease, he said.
Waiting closer to delivery can improve pricing, Hytinen said, while pre-leasing helps ensure facilities meet tenants’ specifications. He cited cash-on-cash levered returns of approximately 10% to 12%, with higher returns in India.
Records business supports investment
Hytinen said Iron Mountain expects organic physical records volume to rise modestly, generally by 0.2% to 0.7% annually. The company plans to consolidate its approximately 1,400 warehouses over the long term to improve efficiency and lower costs.
He described the records business as a source of cash flow for investment in growth areas. Michael Burry, the investor best known for betting against the U.S. housing market before the 2008 financial crisis, just bought more Adobe (ADBE -4.25%). In a post for subscribers to his Substack newsletter on Monday, Nov. 16, Burry wrote he added to his stake at about $246 a share. He also said Adobe is now a full position for him.
The next day, the creative software company's shares are even cheaper, down about 4% on Tuesday to roughly $235 as of this writing. This leaves it under what Burry paid, and about two-thirds below the stock's record close in November 2021.
Burry listed two risks to his own case: the cost of using outside artificial intelligence (AI) models, and slower growth in new subscriptions. Adobe's latest numbers show signs of both.
But I think he's right anyway, and the lower price only makes his case stronger.
Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.
Free tools haven't stopped Adobe
Burry didn't just find the stock. In an April post on his Substack, he put Adobe near the top of the software and payments firms he tracks.
On Monday, he said he still thinks Adobe will adjust to AI. He acknowledged that Adobe is often held up as the software company most threatened by AI, pointing to ArtCraft, a free AI-coded clone of seven Adobe apps that has been getting attention.
His answer, according to reports on his paywalled post, is that free alternatives to tools like Photoshop have been around for decades. But Adobe has grown revenue at least 10% in each of the last four years. He credited the company's standard file formats, its big base of current users, its enterprise contracts, and its information security -- not better AI models.
Adobe's own results back up the growth claim. Revenue rose 10% to $19.4 billion in fiscal 2023, then 11% to $21.5 billion in fiscal 2024 and 11% to $23.8 billion in fiscal 2025. What's more, growth has sped up a bit this year. Revenue climbed 13% year over year to a record $6.76 billion in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ended Aug. 28, 2026). And management's target for the full fiscal year, which ends this month, points to growth of around 12%.
Are AI costs catching up with Adobe?
Burry's first risk shows up more clearly in the numbers. Adobe offers its own AI models along with partners' models, and it doesn't share what it pays outside providers. But the cost of its subscription revenue, which is mainly third-party hosting and data center costs (including the cost of running AI features), is rising fast.
That cost rose 10% year over year in the fiscal first quarter. It grew faster in each of the next two quarters, by 16% and then by 24%. Subscription revenue, meanwhile, climbed 13% to 14% in each of those quarters. In other words, the cost of serving subscribers has risen faster every quarter this fiscal year, but subscription sales have grown at a steady pace.
Granted, that cost started from a low base. Around 90 cents of every subscription dollar was still left after covering it in fiscal Q3, compared to about 91 cents a year before. But if the acceleration continues, it might keep chipping away at Adobe's profit margins.

As I write this, it is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. This past weekend was a gold mine for running fans. On Friday and Saturday, October 30 and 31, NCAA Division I Cross-Country Conference Championships took place in various locations across the United States. The competition was deep and fast, and we were treated to a preview of key matchups we will see at the national championships in a few weeks.
The Javelina 100 Mile also took place in Arizona’s McDowell Mountain Regional Park. Judging by the finish times — and despite heavy rains — it appears the front group of runners sprinted for a full 100 miles. In the women’s race, the victory was decided by a mere 56 seconds — a margin of victory that fills me with empathetic distress.
Then on Sunday, more than 61,000 runners took to the streets for the New York City Marathon. We watched epic throwdowns, including Sweden’s Andreas Almgren victory in his debut marathon, and American Jessica McClain came away with a brilliant runner-up finish over the final strides in the women’s race. These are exciting times to be a running fan.
The races themselves were great — the striving and struggling, camaraderie, mud, and the beauty of trying hard (1). But post-race interviews are always my favorite part of big race weekends. These interviews are often drenched in gratitude for good health and the opportunity to compete, for competitors, and for the people who supported their efforts along the way. We hear about families, friends, and volunteers. Athletes often speak in terms of “we” instead of “I.”
It is perhaps surprising that many of the biggest moments of a runner’s career are accompanied by expressions of gratitude. Instead of keeping the focus on themselves, they direct it to others. They win and are given a platform to speak. Then they use this platform to say, “Thank you (2).”
The Concept
Gratitude is a virtue of appreciation that involves recognizing that we have received some good or benefit. For runners, this “good” can mean the expertise of physical trainers, the company of running buddies, the encouragement of family members, or care from aid station volunteers. This recognition involves actions, thoughts, and emotions (3). Grateful people “behave in a thankful way towards their benefactors, but also have appropriate feelings of positive appreciation and regard for them (4).”
Gratitude involves a “to-for” structure: “We are thankful to someone for some gratuitous good (5).” This structure makes gratitude corrective of tendencies toward entitlement and thanklessness. Cheshire Calhoun writes that what makes gratitude a virtue is, in part, that it “corrects a tendency not to attend to the benefactor but instead simply to enjoy the benefit (6).” In other words, gratitude recognizes that others play a role in our flourishing and in the goods we possess. In this way, gratitude is an antidote to egoism and presumption about our independent contributions to outcomes.
Why does gratitude matter for runners? There are at least three reasons.

Finnish satellite operator ICEYE made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket maker Avio on Tuesday, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defense group.
The deal fits with efforts to reduce reliance on external providers and narrow a widening gap with industry leaders in the US and China.
ICEYE said its €41-per-share offer will be launched through wholly owned Italian subsidiary Iris 2 with the aim of delisting the company. Avio shares climbed more than 15% to around €39.5 on the news.
“Europe’s need for sovereign space and defense capabilities is growing. Building the industrial capacity to meet that demand takes years, which makes it critical to invest now,” said ICEYE, which intends to fund the offer with cash and debt.
ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with satellite radar imagery since 2022, and last month signed a letter of intent with Nokia and Ukraine’s Defence Ministry to explore cooperation in space, including sovereign satellite communications.
“If completed … a global space industry player will be created, through which the self-sufficient security of supply of Finland’s and all of Europe‘s defense will rise to a new level,” said Finnish defense minister Antti Hakkanen.
Investments in Italy
State-backed ICEYE said it intends to invest an additional €1 billion in Italy over five years after the potential deal is completed, seeking to increase the launch cadence and expand the customer base of Avio’s Vega rocket.
Avio‘s board held a first meeting on Tuesday and said it had started assessing the bid, which ICEYE said offered a 21.3% premium to the Italian group’s closing price on Monday or a 34.8% premium to its three-month volume-weighted average price.
Speaking at an event in Helsinki, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction.
The deal will need several regulatory approvals, including an official green light from the Italian government as Avio is seen as a strategic asset under Rome’s golden power rules.
The CEO of Italian defense group Leonardo, a key Avio shareholder with an 18% stake, said he was “pleasantly surprised” by the bid and would examine it, in coordination with the government.
European Champion
The deal would pair Avio’s launch and propulsion capabilities with the satellite manufacturing, constellation operations and intelligence services of ICEYE, which was founded in 2014 and provides radar satellite imagery to Western governments and militaries.
“It’s a phenomenal combination of capabilities… bringing a full vertical integration, following quite clear industry trends,” Modrzewski said, adding that it would be beneficial for both companies.
The Finnish group said it intends to preserve Avio’s brand, retain its existing workforce and continue its planned investments in the United States.
As part of its push into the US defense market, Avio is building a manufacturing plant in Virginia, which it expects to complete in late 2028.

New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies.
According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia.
Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions, the rule said.
The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models.
U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers.
About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank.
The buildout has come under greater scrutiny as Washington presses ahead with the investigation into Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang left the company that he co-founded in 1993 after reports of several alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy who is believed to facilitate billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips into China.
The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said.
Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.
Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out.
Who are most exposed?
Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers.
More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.
Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said.
"Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle," she said, potentially knocking 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028.
Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny.

The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.
October's reading puts U.K. inflation at a one-year high.
Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated.
The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September.
Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
